title: The still small voice
hookLine: not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–12)

cards: Elijah is done. In the book of Kings, Queen Jezebel has sworn to kill the prophet. He runs into the wilderness, sits under a juniper tree, and asks to die.
An angel wakes him and feeds him, and he walks on until he reaches a mountain and goes into a cave. There a voice asks him a strange question: "What doest thou here, Elijah?"
Then he's told to go out and stand on the mountain, because the LORD is about to pass by.

teach.h: NOT IN THE WIND, QUAKE OR FIRE.

teach.b: In the King James words: "and, behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake".
Then a fire, and again: not in the fire. Wind, earthquake, fire: the things that usually announce power. Each one arrives, and each one is empty.
Second, the quiet: "and after the fire a still small voice." No thunder, no blaze. Some readers hear the Hebrew as something even quieter than a voice: a thin silence.
Whatever it was, it was small. Third, Elijah's response. He's been through the wind and the earthquake, but it's the quiet that moves him.
When Elijah heard it, the text says, he wrapped his face in his mantle and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave. Awe, here, comes in at a whisper. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day.
A lot of life is wind and earthquake and fire: notifications, headlines, arguments, alarms.
The story suggests that what matters most may not be the loudest thing in the room. For Jews and Christians, this is about how God speaks.
For anyone, it's an invitation to make enough quiet to hear something small.

how: Jews and Christians read Elijah's story in 1 Kings 19 as a teaching about how God speaks; some people take it as a reason to sit in silence and listen.

o: a king of Israel who built the first temple
the angel who fed a prophet in the desert
the prophet who heard God in a still small voice

games.q: Elijah on the mountain — tap the pairs.
p: rent the mountains; the LORD not in it
wrapped his face in his mantle

s: the LORD was in the earthquake
"the LORD was not in the earthquake."
Elijah came to the mountain full of confidence
he had fled into the wilderness and asked to die.
when Elijah heard the quiet, he wrapped his face in his mantle
it was the quiet, not the noise, that moved him.

games.q: you're Elijah. wind, then earthquake, then fire have passed. now there is a still small voice. what do you do?
o: fall flat on the ground in fear.
wrap your face in your mantle and go to the cave's mouth.
games.why: he wraps his face in his mantle and goes out to stand at the entrance of the cave. the whisper moves him more than the fire did.

practice: Close your eyes if you like, and notice the loud things first, traffic, voices in another room, your own busy thoughts, letting each one pass by like Elijah's wind.
Then listen underneath for the quietest thing you can find: your breath, the hum of the room, the small silence between two sounds.
If you pray, listen the way Elijah did, with nothing to say, and stay a minute past the bell if you'd like.

wordCard.voice: Elijah. The prophet who heard, after the wind, the earthquake and the fire, a quiet so small it moved him more than all the noise. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, from 1 Kings 19:12: rendered still small voice; some readers hear a thin silence.
